title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
hook: a girl tries on the garland meant for the god

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kamsa's death: the king whose fear kept his mind on Krishna all his life, pulled down in his own arena, and a prison door opening for Devaki and Vasudeva. What did your mind keep circling yesterday? Day nine hundred seven.

A garland of fresh flowers lies ready in a temple gardener's house, woven that morning for the image of Vishnu. While her father is out, his daughter picks it up. She puts it around her own neck. Then she leans over to see her reflection, and asks herself a question: would he want me? Except the he, for her, is the god the garland was made for. Today the path leaves the Bhagavata's village and meets the people who sang about it, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A GARLAND FOR THE GOD.` → `SHE TRIES IT ON FIRST.` → `WOULD HE WANT ME?`

segments.voice: The Alvars are the poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil. Tradition counts twelve of them, and explains the name as people who are immersed, sunk deep in God, the way you sink into water over your head. Their songs are not theology lectures. They are love songs, complaints, lullabies, longing. The girl with the garland is one of them. Her name is Andal. The story told about her goes like this. Her father, himself remembered as one of the Alvars, tends a flower garden for the temple. Tradition says he found her there as a baby, under a tulasi plant, and raised her as his own. She grows up on his stories of Krishna, and somewhere along the way she decides she will marry no one but the Lord. So she wears the garland before it goes to the temple. One day her father catches her. He's horrified: a garland someone has already worn can't be offered to God. He throws it out and weaves a new one. That night, the story says, the Lord comes to him in a dream and asks why the usual garland didn't arrive. The one she wore is the one he wants. From then on, her garlands go to the temple after she has worn them, and she gets a name for it: the girl who gave the garland she had worn. Sit with how strange that is. The rule of offering says fresh and untouched. And the story says God prefers the flowers that have already been warm against someone's neck, someone who loved him enough to try them on. The other name in today's title, Nammalvar, comes the day after tomorrow. Today it's enough to meet a gardener's daughter and a garland.
screen: `THE ALVARS: POETS SUNK DEEP IN GOD.` · `A BABY UNDER THE TULASI PLANT.` · `HER FATHER THROWS THE GARLAND OUT.` · `THE ONE SHE WORE IS THE ONE HE WANTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of something you give that isn't brand new: your tired attention at the end of a day, a meal you've made a hundred times, a phone call when you're half asleep. The kind of offering you might be tempted to throw out and redo. Hold it for a moment without fixing it. If you pray, you can offer it as it is, worn and warm, to God by whatever name you use. If you don't, simply notice that it was given. The bell holds the time.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu, whose name tradition explains as those sunk deep in God. Andal is the one who wore the garland first.
Your line: the garland she wore first. Today, give one thing as it is, a little used and still warm, instead of waiting until it's perfect. Day nine hundred seven.

howItsDone: Andal is honored as one of the Alvars in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes; at Srivilliputtur, tradition holds that a garland worn by her image is still offered to the Lord.
